title: When the Ledger Falls
premise: In the winter of 1918, Wren Ashgrove keeps the light at Gullwrack Point while the great storms batter the coast and the war grinds toward an uncertain armistice. When a drowned courier washes ashore carrying a sealed letter naming the Ashgroves as keepers of a promise made in peacetime — safe passage for a man now declared enemy — Wren must choose between duty to the Crown, survival for her children, and a debt of honor no one else will honor. As naval investigators close in and the storms cut the point off from help, Wren shelters the enemy soldier her late husband swore to protect, discovering he carries proof that could end the war weeks early or damn her family forever. In the climax she burns the ledger that would expose them all, trading truth for mercy; the armistice comes, and Wren keeps the lighthouse with the knowledge that some promises outlast nations.
about_author: Ada Okafor is a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse keepers' logs from the First World War era. She writes historical fiction about ordinary people caught in the machinery of empire, and lives within sight of a decommissioned light station.

chapters.title: The Weight of Oil and Salt
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Establishes daily life at Gullwrack Point: trimming wicks, rationing oil, raising two children alone since her husband Edmund's death at sea. The great storms begin earlier than any log records. Emotional beat: weary competence masking grief, and the quiet dread that the war will reach even this rock.

chapters.title: What the Sea Returns
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. After the worst storm of the season, a body washes into the cove clutching a waterproof satchel: a sealed letter addressed to 'E. Ashgrove, Keeper.' Edmund has been dead eight months. Wren reads it by lamplight and learns of a promise made before the war. Emotional beat: shock curdling into fear as she realizes her husband bound her to something dangerous.

chapters.title: A Debt Signed in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with flashback to 1913. The letter reveals Edmund sheltered a foreign engineer, Lukas Brandt, during a shipwreck years ago and swore the light would always burn for him. Now Brandt is classified an enemy national. Wren must decide whether to answer the letter's request to signal his arrival. Emotional beat: love against duty begins its quiet war inside her.

chapters.title: The Inspector's Coat
chapters.summary: Inspector Hale's POV. A naval investigator arrives on the supply boat, ostensibly checking storm damage to coastal signals, actually hunting a missing courier whose dispatch case never reached Whitehall. He notes the Ashgrove children's German primer and files it away. Emotional beat: polite menace; the reader sees the trap closing that Wren cannot yet.

chapters.title: Signal Fires
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Against every instinct, Wren answers the letter: three short flashes on the agreed night. Her daughter Maren catches her at the lamp and says nothing, becoming a silent accomplice. Days later, a half-frozen man appears at the door. Emotional beat: terror and strange exhilaration — the point of no return crossed.

chapters.title: The Man Beneath the Enemy's Name
chapters.summary: Alternating Wren and Brandt POV. Brandt recovers in the boathouse; he is not a spy but a cartographer carrying charts proving the enemy fleet's mined channels — intelligence that could save thousands if it reaches the right hands, or hang him if intercepted. Wren and Brandt argue over what honor requires now. Emotional beat: wary respect kindling into something warmer neither will name.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Treasons
chapters.summary: Maren's POV (age twelve). The child's-eye view of complicity: extra bread vanishing, her mother lying smoothly to Inspector Hale over tea, her brother asking why they can't just tell the truth. Maren copies entries from her father's old keeper's ledger and understands, for the first time, what her parents were. Emotional beat: lost innocence, fierce loyalty.

chapters.title: The Storm That Eats the Light
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The greatest storm of the year strikes; the lamp mechanism fails mid-blow, and a naval patrol vessel founders on the rocks within sight of the dark tower. Wren and Brandt work side by side through the night to relight it, saving sailors including men from Hale's own search party. Emotional beat: the enemy becomes a rescuer; duty and betrayal blur beyond recognition.

chapters.title: Armistice Eve
chapters.summary: Hale's POV turning to Wren's. Hale knows — the rescued sailors described the man who saved them. But with rumors of armistice sweeping the coast, prosecuting a rescuer is politically impossible. He offers Wren a bargain: surrender the charts, and the Ashgroves vanish from his report. Climax: Wren instead burns the ledger and the letter, destroying all written proof, and gives Hale the charts freely — choosing mercy over leverage. Emotional beat: sacrifice as power.

chapters.title: Keeping the Light
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, months later. The armistice signed; Brandt repatriated, leaving behind a promise to return when passports allow. The Ashgroves remain keepers of Gullwrack, poorer in secrets but richer in knowing exactly what they are. Final image: Wren trims the wick at dusk and thinks of Edmund, understanding at last the price of the promise — and that she would pay it again. Emotional beat: hard-won peace, love enduring against everything.
